mainEntity.name: What is the best kanban tool with an API for developers?

acceptedAnswer.text: Hypertask is our top pick for developers coordinating humans, scripts, and external AI agents. Linear fits engineering issue workflows; GitHub Projects fits work already tracked through GitHub issues and pull requests. Choose based on the workflow, not the number of endpoints.

mainEntity.name: Does Hypertask have a REST API or only MCP?

acceptedAnswer.text: Hypertask has a public REST API at https://app.hypertask.ai/api/v1, alongside its first-party CLI and MCP server. REST requests use bearer API keys and JSON. Descriptions, comments, and drafts use HTML, so convert Markdown before sending those fields.

mainEntity.name: Is MCP the same as a kanban API?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. MCP lets compatible AI clients discover and call tools. REST and GraphQL are HTTP API styles your application can use directly. They may expose different capabilities, so check the documented interface rather than assuming feature parity.

mainEntity.name: Which kanban tools have a free plan with API access?

acceptedAnswer.text: Hypertask, Linear, Trello, GitHub Projects, and Jira offer free entry plans and documented programmatic access. Free plans still have product limits, API quotas, or related compute costs. Test your intended workload before treating free access as unlimited automation.

mainEntity.name: Can Hypertask automatically sync GitHub issues and pull requests?

acceptedAnswer.text: The public Hypertask documentation reviewed for this article does not describe native GitHub issue or pull-request synchronization. You can link code evidence on a task or build a custom integration. Choose GitHub Projects if native issue and pull-request connection is your main requirement.

Hypertask is our top pick for the best kanban tool with an API when developers want scripts and AI agents working on the same board as humans.
Its documented REST API, first-party CLI, and MCP server let software read and update tasks while people review the results in context.

If you only need a cheap visual board, Trello may fit better. If every task is a GitHub issue, GitHub Projects deserves the first test. The right API is the one that removes manual relay work without creating another system to maintain.
What makes a kanban API useful?
Moving a card is the easy part. Useful automation also needs to read the task description, identify its owner, post evidence, and hand the result to a reviewer.

That distinction comes from real customer conversations. Technical teams describe scattered TODO files, agent work hidden in terminal sessions, and decisions split between the board and chat. They do not need another status dashboard. They need to know what happened and what needs a decision.

The 5 best kanban tools with an API
1. Hypertask: best for humans, scripts, and AI agents sharing a board
Developers and technical founders who want a task to survive beyond a terminal session, with a visible owner and review step.

Agents using their own bearer tokens have their writes attributed to the agent rather than the human owner. That matters when you need to distinguish a teammate’s decision from an automated update.

These interfaces are not interchangeable. The docs identify worker infrastructure such as leases, evidence, and escalation as REST-only, rather than ordinary MCP tools. Task descriptions and comments use HTML, not Markdown. Plan your integration around the documented surface you actually need.
The public docs reviewed do not describe a native GitHub issue or pull-request synchronization integration. Do not assume linking a pull request means its status will sync automatically.

2. Linear: best for an engineering issue workflow
Product and engineering teams that want issues, projects, and cycles rather than a general-purpose card system.

supports personal API keys and OAuth, with a first-party TypeScript SDK. You can fetch exactly the fields you need and create or update issues through mutations. Linear recommends webhooks for receiving changes instead of repeatedly downloading the whole backlog.

GraphQL adds a learning step if your scripts expect simple REST endpoints. A successful HTTP response can still contain GraphQL errors. Linear also applies both request and query-complexity limits, so large nested queries need care. Its
is essential reading before building a sync worker.

lists Free with two teams and 250 issues. Basic is $10 per user per month billed yearly; Business is $16. The comparison includes API and webhook access, but free issue limits can become the practical constraint.
3. Trello: best for simple REST-based card automation
Small teams that want recognizable cards and lists, with scripts handling repeatable board chores.

walks through keys, tokens, boards, and cards. Its card-and-list model is straightforward to map into a small integration. Built-in automation and Power-Ups may also remove the need to write code for basic rules.
Your integration still needs to define what ownership, evidence, and review mean. Trello’s flexibility does not enforce your operating process. Its
include 300 requests per ten seconds per API key and 100 per ten seconds per token, with additional limits for some resources.

lists Free for up to ten collaborators and ten boards per Workspace. Standard is $5 per user per month billed annually; Premium is $10. Built-in automation quotas are separate from REST API rate limits.

4. GitHub Projects: best when the work already lives in GitHub
Developers whose source of truth is GitHub issues and pull requests, especially when automation already runs in GitHub Actions.

supports board, table, and roadmap views over issues and pull requests. Changes to those underlying records stay connected to the project. GitHub documents GraphQL and Actions as ways to automate project behavior.
That avoids building a second issue-sync layer just to see code work on a board.

Projects automation uses GraphQL; an existing issue REST script does not automatically cover project fields and items. The workflow also assumes collaborators are comfortable working in GitHub. That can be a poor fit for clients or nontechnical colleagues who only need assignments and approvals.
includes Issues and Projects in Free. Actions, hosted compute, and other paid services have their own allowances and costs. A free board does not make every automation job free.
5. Jira: best for teams needing detailed workflow controls
Organizations already using Jira, or teams whose permissions and workflow requirements justify a more configurable system.
. The API supports issue operations, search, and integrations subject to the caller’s permissions.
let integrations respond to changes instead of relying entirely on polling.

Configuration is part of the integration. Field formats, workflow transitions, scopes, and project permissions need explicit handling. Jira REST API v3 uses Atlassian Document Format for rich text in several fields, including descriptions and comment bodies. Do not treat moving an issue as a generic status-string update.
offers Free for ten users, followed by Standard, Premium, and Enterprise. Use its current seat calculator for paid pricing rather than assuming one flat rate at every team size.

How to set up API automation in Hypertask
Start with one board and one harmless read request. Prove access before allowing a worker to modify real tasks.
1. Create the board and a review column
Create a board with Backlog, Doing, Review, and Done. Treat these as your team’s chosen column names, not mandatory system defaults.
Give each task an owner and a clear completion condition. Keep human approval in Review so a script cannot accidentally equate passing tests with permission to ship.
